articles.title: New Paper: Does the P3b component reflect working memory updating?
articles.content:
Carrasco, C. D., Simmons, A. M., Kiat, J. E., & Luck, S. J. (in press). Enhanced working memory representations for rare events. Psychophysiology. https://doi.org/10.1111/psyp.70038 [preprint]

For decades, many ERP researchers have believed that the P3b wave (sometimes called P300) is a scalp manifestation of a process that updates working memory. This idea originated with Manny Donchin’s context updating hypothesis of the P3b (Donchin, 1981). Donchin’s idea of context was pretty different from working memory, but as this hypothesis percolated through the field over time, it gradually morphed into the idea that the P3b reflects the updating of working memory.

Rolf Verleger mounted a major attack on the original context updating hypothesis in a classic review article in BBS (Verleger, 1988), which was followed by a vigorous rebuttal by Donchin and Coles (1988). These are interesting papers to read, but they did not settle the issue. In the ensuing years, as the field became more focused on working memory instead of context, I’m aware of no studies that directly tested the hypothesis that the P3b reflects working memory updating.

One reason for the lack of direct evidence is that the oddball paradigms typically used to elicit the P3b do not provide a sensitive assessment of working memory. In a typical paradigm, for example, participants would see a sequence of 90% Xs and 10% Os, and the task would be to press one button for X and another button for O. The responses are made immediately, so it is not necessary to store the stimuli in working memory. Even if participants were asked to make a delayed response, the Xs and Os are so easily discriminable that memory performance would likely be at ceiling.

A few years ago, my lab (especially Carlos Carrasco, Aaron Simmons, and John Kiat) got interested in trying to test the working memory encoding hypothesis. We ran a couple of experiments, but we couldn’t quite figure out the right design. Finally, we figured it out. We used a modified oddball paradigm in which a little dot appeared at one of many locations around an circle (see Figure 1).

On each trial, participants pressed one button if the circle was close to one of the four cardinal axes (left, right, top, and bottom) and a different button if it was close to one of the four diagonals (upper left, upper right, lower left, and lower right). One of these two categories was rare (the oddballs) and the other was frequent (the standards; counterbalanced across trial blocks). As is usual in oddball paradigms, the P3b was much larger for trials in the rare category than for trials in the frequent category (see Figure 2).

The main question was whether the location of the dot was encoded in working memory better for the oddball trials than for the standard trials. To assess this, the experimental design contained occasional probe trials on which participants used the mouse to click on the exact location of the dot (see Figure 3). That is, after participants made the cardinal/diagonal buttonpress responses, they were sometimes then asked to click on the remembered location of the dot. This happened on only 12.5% of trials, selected at random, so that participants would mainly focus on the oddball task.

We looked at the accuracy of these probe responses, calculated as the (absolute value of the) angular distance between the true location and the reported location. As shown in Figure 4, the response error of the probe responses was reduced for the oddball trials relative to the standard trials. In other words, working memory was better for the P3b-eliciting oddball trials than for the standards. Moreover, we found that participants with large P3b amplitudes on oddball trials had smaller response errors on oddball trials (whereas this correlation was not present for standards).

At first glance, these findings seem like support for the idea that the P3b reflects working memory updating. However, the story is not that simple. For example, when we looked at single-trial P3b amplitudes, response errors were not lower for trials with larger P3b amplitudes than for trials with smaller P3b amplitudes.

We also used ERP decoding to test whether the exact location of the dot was better stored in working memory on oddball trials than on standard trials (click here for information about how ERP decoding works and how you can decode your own data using ERPLAB Toolbox). As shown in Figure 5, we could decode the location of the dot better on oddball trials than on standard trials during the period following the P3b component. Note, however, that this was a pretty small difference that only barely crossed the threshold for statistical significance (p = .048). I would really like to see this effect replicated before fully believing it. However, the behavioral effect was rock solid (and replicated in a follow-up experiment).

What can we conclude from these findings? When we started the project, I knew that it would be difficult to draw any strong causal conclusions about the relationship between the P3b component and working memory updating. That is, even if we saw both a larger P3b and improved working memory on oddball trials, this would just be a correlation and could potentially be explained by a third variable such as attention. But if we saw a big difference in working memory between oddballs and standards, and if we found that working memory was better on trials with larger P3b amplitudes, this would be at least consistent with the idea that the process that produces the P3b on the scalp is also involved in working memory encoding.

However, although we saw an enormous difference in P3b amplitude between oddball trials and standard trials, we saw only small differences in working memory between oddballs and standards, whether measured via behavioral response errors on probe trials or EEG decoding accuracy. If the process that generates the scalp P3b voltage plays a major role in working memory encoding, then we would have expected a much larger working memory difference between oddballs and standards. Moreover, although we found that participants with larger P3b amplitudes had smaller response errors, we did not find any evidence that working memory was any better on trials with larger P3b amplitudes (even though we looked very hard for such a relationship). The bottom line is that, although I was really hoping we would finally provide some direct evidence for the working memory encoding hypothesis, the results of this study have actually convinced me that the P3b is probably not related to working memory encoding.

What, then, explains the small but statistically significant differences in working memory accuracy between oddballs and standards, along with the subjectwise correlation between P3b amplitude and behavioral response errors? A very plausible explanation is that both the P3b component and working memory encoding are facilitated by increased attention. That is, there are several sources of evidence that rare events trigger increased attention, and this could independently produce a larger P3b and improved working memory.

Of course, this is just one experiment, so I wouldn’t say that the working memory encoding hypothesis is completely dead. But given our new findings and the general lack of direct evidence for the hypothesis, it’s on life support.

If the P3b doesn’t reflect working memory encoding, then what does it reflect? This seems like a significant question: the P3b is huge and is observed across a broad range of experimental paradigms, and it’s reasonable to assume that the underlying process must be important for the brain to devote so many watts of energy to it. In fact, I find it embarrassing that our field has not answered this question in the 60 years since the P3b was first discovered.

My best bet is that the P3b is related to the process of making decisions about actions (where the term actions is broadly construed to include the withholding of responses and mental actions such as counting). This is related to the fact that the amplitude of the P3b is related to the probability of a task-defined category, not the probability of a physical stimulus category. Rolf Verleger has a nice review of the evidence for this idea (Verleger, 2020). But it is still not clear to me why the brain devotes so many watts of energy to creating a large P3b when a rare task-defined category occurs. Verleger notes that several hypotheses about the P3b are compatible with the finding of a larger P3b for oddballs than for standards, but in my view these hypotheses have a hard time explaining the enormous size of the P3b observed for oddballs. This is a longstanding mystery in need of a solution!

articles.title: 10-Day ERP Boot Camp to be held June 15-24, 2026 in Davis, California
articles.content:
We have received another 5 years of funding from the National Institute of Mental Health, so we plan to hold ERP Boot Camps in each of the next 5 summers. The next one will be June 15-24, 2026 in Davis, California. The application portal will open around January 1, 2026.

As in most previous years, all attendees will receive a scholarship that covers most or all travel and lodging expenses. There will be no registration fee.

Click here for more information about the ERP Boot Camp.

If you would like to receive announcements about upcoming boot camps, join our email list. If you have any questions after reading this page and the application information page, please email us at erpbootcamp@gmail.com.

articles.title: A Reproducible Cortical Model of Focal Epileptiform Activity with a Multi-Biomarker Analysis Pipeline
articles.content: The development of surface-based therapeutic strategies, including extracranial illumination and epicortical electrical or optoelectronic neuromodulation, requires experimental models in which focal pathological activity can be generated and monitored within an accessible cortical region. Here, we established an acute cortical model of focal epileptiform activity in anesthetized mice based on local microinjection of 4-aminopyridine (4-AP) into the barrel cortex. This preparation provides precise spatial and temporal control of the epileptiform focus while enabling simultaneous electrophysiological sampling across cortical depth. To objectively characterize the induced activity, we implemented a Python-based analysis pipeline integrating complementary electrophysiological biomarkers, including oscillatory power, multi-unit activity, pathological fast ripples (250-650 Hz), and epileptiform bursts. Local 4-AP administration produced robust increases in gamma (30-100 Hz) power, multi-unit firing (MUA), fast ripple and burst activity. Pharmacological sensitivity of the framework was evaluated using carbamazepine, which robustly attenuated 4-AP-induced increases in all biomarkers. Together, this study provides a reproducible experimental and analytical framework for investigating focal cortical epileptiform activity and for the future evaluation of pharmacological, optical, and electrical interventions targeting superficial cortical networks.
articles.author: Lopez-Cabezon, C., Gener, T. A., Polo-Rodriguez, A., Puig, M. V.

articles.title: The role of world knowledge in sentence comprehension under working-memory constraints: An fMRI study
articles.content: Introduction: Comprehension of thematic roles, i.e., "who did what to whom," relies on limited cognitive resources, and constraints on these resources can alter the use of plausibility information derived from world knowledge. Although sentence-processing studies have described how plausibility information constrains interpretation, it remains unclear how this process is supported by the architecture of working memory. This study examines whether the phonological loop, one of the components of working memory, contributes to thematic-role processing based on world knowledge. Methods: Using articulatory suppression and functional magnetic resonance imaging, we examined whether constraining the function of the phonological loop modulates behavioral and neural responses to sentences in which syntactically assigned thematic roles are plausible or implausible given world knowledge. To constrain the phonological loop, we manipulated the task: a single task and a dual task involving concurrent articulation. Results: We found no significant interaction between task and plausibility, although equivalence analyses did not provide evidence for the absence of a plausibility effect during articulation. In contrast, a robust main effect of thematic-role plausibility was observed: implausible sentences elicited greater activation than plausible sentences in the left inferior frontal gyrus (LIFG) and medial superior frontal gyrus (mSFG) at the whole-brain level, and in both the pars triangularis and pars orbitalis of the LIFG in the ROI analyses. Discussion: These findings provide no conclusive evidence that constraining the phonological loop substantially modulates the use of world knowledge in comprehension of thematic roles, while also leaving open the possibility of a smaller task-dependent effect. At the same time, the robust neural responses to implausibility indicate that the LIFG and mSFG consistently contribute to the processing of plausibility information derived from world knowledge.

Cross-modal alignment with language tokens for unified multilingual image-to-text generation
articles.content: Current multimodal translation systems typically employ a cascaded pipeline where image captioning and machine translation are performed sequentially, leading to error propagation and semantic drift. This paper introduces a unified neural architecture that integrates visual encoding, English caption generation and multilingual translation into a single end-to-end model. Our first key contribution is this unified framework which jointly optimizes both tasks through shared latent representations enabling richer cross-modal learning and more semantically consistent multilingual outputs than conventional systems. The architecture incorporates two core technical innovations. First, we introduce a cross-modal representation alignment mechanism that directly fuses hierarchical visual features from a CNN encoder with multilingual linguistic embeddings in the Transformer decoder. This ensures visual semantics (e.g., gender, count, and object attributes) are preserved during translation effectively grounding multilingual outputs in the visual context and rectifying a common failure mode of text-only NMT. Second, we design a language token driven conditioning strategy prepending learnable target language tokens to guide a single multilingual model. This allows dynamic adaptation to diverse syntax and morphology without requiring separate decoders for each language. Empirical evaluations on MS COCO and OPUS multilingual datasets demonstrate notable improvements over existing multimodal and cascaded baselines achieving a BLEU-4 score of 44.8 for English captioning and an average BLEU of 41.1 across five target languages (Chinese, French, Arabic, Spanish, and Hindi), representing gains of 2.2 and 2.0 points, respectively, over cascaded baselines. COMET scores averaging 0.732 further confirm the semantic fidelity of our visually grounded translations. The proposed framework establishes a scalable, visually grounded and linguistically adaptive solution for multilingual caption generation contributing a meaningful advancement toward integrated vision-language translation research and real-world accessibility applications.
articles.author: Guanjun Lin

articles.title: Mapping the natural course of comorbid bipolar disorder via integration of multimodal data (MapCoBD): a study protocol
articles.content: BackgroundBipolar disorder (BD) is a chronic, disabling psychiatric condition with a high global disease burden. Its course is marked by alternating episodes of mania and depression, with varying degrees of severity. While cyclicity is a defining feature, clinical patterns show significant inter-individual and intra-individual variability. Although naturalistic studies have described the course of BD, the impact of psychiatric comorbidities, particularly attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and borderline personality disorder (BPD), remains underexplored. MapCoBD is a 12-month, naturalistic observational study whose primary objective is to compare the longitudinal clinical course of BD among individuals with classic episodic BD, BD with comorbid ADHD, and BD with comorbid BPD. Secondary objectives are to characterize the clinical, neuropsychological, neuroimaging, and molecular features associated with these distinct clinical courses.ContentThis project will recruit 150 BD individuals divided into three groups: (1) classic episodic BD (epiBD, n = 50), (2) BD with comorbid ADHD (BD-ADHD, n = 50), and (3) BD with comorbid BPD (BD-BPD, n = 50). Assessments will be conducted at baseline (T0), 6 months (T1), and 12 months (T2), including: mood symptom ratings, neuropsychological testing, fasting blood sampling (for serum, plasma, and microRNA), and 3T structural brain MRI scans. Daily mood ratings will also be collected prospectively throughout the study. The primary longitudinal clinical endpoint will be illness burden, defined as the proportion of evaluable follow-up days spent with moderate-to-severe psychopathological symptoms, based on prospective NIMH Life Chart Method assessments. Daily affective ratings will additionally be used to characterize mood instability. At each time point, peripheral biomarkers implicated in BD pathophysiology, including endocannabinoid (eCB) signaling, inflammatory cascade (IC), and epigenetic regulation (microRNA), will be quantified. Clinical, neuroimaging, and molecular data will also be integrated using supervised machine-learning approaches to explore the classification of clinical group status and the prediction of longitudinal mood instability and illness burden.ConclusionsThis study will determine whether ADHD and BPD comorbidity is associated with distinct longitudinal patterns of illness burden and mood instability in BD. The integration of clinical, neuroimaging, and molecular data may identify group-specific multimodal signatures and candidate predictors of clinical course, which will require independent validation before clinical application.
articles.author: Mirko Manchia

articles.title: Federated Spiking GANs with Rényi Differential Privacy for privacy-preserving synthetic EEG generation in brain–computer interfaces
articles.content: Electroencephalography (EEG) data used in brain-computer and brain-machine interfaces (BCI/BMI) contain sensitive, user-specific information, creating privacy risks in consumer applications such as gaming, human augmentation, and virtual reality. Existing methods like encryption and anonymization either fail to protect data during analysis or still expose identifiable attributes. While differential privacy (DP) offers formal protection, it often reduces data utility. The key challenge is to generate synthetic EEG data that protects sensitive attributes while retaining temporal features for downstream use. To address this, we developed a federated spiking generative framework that integrates a spiking neural network (SNN)-based generator, temporally correlated noise, an artificial neural network (ANN)-based discriminator, and Rényi differential privacy (RDP) within a federated learning framework. The SNN-based generator captures temporal characteristics, and the ANN-based discriminator maintains classification accuracy. Federated training prevents centralization of raw client data, while privacy is preserved through controlled perturbation of spike-train and membrane-potential representations, supported by RDP-based privacy accounting. We evaluated our architecture against methods such as RDP-TimeGAN, RDP-CRNN-GAN, RDP-RCGAN, and RDP-Clare-GAN, demonstrating that our approach preserves temporal features and downstream utility while maintaining privacy in synthetic EEG generation. This solution enables privacy-preserving generation of distributed synthetic EEG data for BCI/BMI research and development.
articles.author: Garima Bajwa

articles.title: Aging with intellectual disabilities: a study in Portugal about clinical conditions, functionality, and frailty
articles.content: The life expectancy of people with intellectual disabilities (ID) has increased more than that of the general population, demanding a deeper understanding of their health profiles to inform tailored healthy aging interventions. This study aimed to characterize persons with ID aged ≥ 45 years in terms of clinical conditions (degree of ID, comorbidities, and medication), malnutrition risk, functional capacity and frailty. To our knowledge, this is the first study to address this topic in Portugal. A cross-sectional, descriptive-correlational design was used, with a non-probability convenience sampling of 234 individuals with ID aged ≥ 45 years. Questionnaires were completed by organizational mediators, achieving a response rate of 18.5%. The mean age was 53.32 years; 56.4% were male, 97.9% were single, and 98.3% had no children. The main findings are as follows: (i) degree of ID: 52.1% moderate, 25.6% severe, 15% mild and 7.3% profound; (ii) high prevalence of comorbidities; (iii) 38.9% were on five or more medicines (polypharmacy); (iv) 44.9% were at risk of malnutrition and 4.7% were malnourished; (v) 23.1% had total or severe dependence in basic activities of daily living; (vi) 85.5% were severely and 14.5% were moderately dependent in instrumental activities of daily living; and (vii) 46.3% were classified as being frail. Older adults with ID seemed to present complex clinical conditions that required a higher intensity of support. These findings contribute to the continuous development of a model of care tailored to older people with ID, particularly healthy aging interventions.
articles.author: Liliana Sousa

articles.title: A two-stage RAG-LLM pipeline for roadmapping neuroscience research in operational environments
articles.content: IntroductionNeuroscientific research and applications in real world environments are often constrained by limited access, equipment limitations, and high costs. Consequently, robustly selecting constructs to focus effort on is a high-impact task.MethodThis study introduces a two-stage large language model (LLM) pipeline that generates research roadmaps from existing real-world data to inform research priorities in the field, given the state of the art. Stage 1 uses retrieval-augmented generation on operational logs to identify candidate psychological, social, and neurocognitive constructs and map their co-occurrence. Stage 2 evaluates how well these constructs are represented in the literature across four dimensions that commonly inform prioritization: ecological validity, neural correlates, biosensor protocols, and brain computer interface readiness, producing an evidence gap matrix. Pipeline evaluation combined human review, deterministic computations, and human-LLM alignment analysis.ResultsApplying the pipeline to Mars Desert Research Station logs, Stage 1 identified 19 constructs. Stage 2 highlighted critical gaps in neuroimaging and measurement protocols, particularly for social domains, thereby identifying potential research priorities and risks.DiscussionThis methodology offers a generalizable starting point for synthesizing operational logs into actionable research roadmaps, but the evaluation showed it still required human scrutiny.
articles.author: Cara A. Spencer
